newsitem.title: ZAIRE: U.S. envoy meets Zaire's Mobutu, rebels advance.
newsitem.headline: U.S. envoy meets Zaire's Mobutu, rebels advance.

text.p: U.S. envoy Bill Richardson held talks with Zaire's embattled President Mobutu Sese Seko on Tuesday and South Africa said a meeting between Mobutu and rebel leader Laurent Kabila was imminent.

"The talks will take place shortly...It will be a meeting between President Mobutu and Laurent Kabila," Pieter Swanepoel, spokesman for South Africa's Department of Foreign Affairs, told Reuters in Johannesburg.
Kabila's rebels, meanwhile, announced that their frontline units had entered Kikwit, 400 km (250 miles) from the Zairean capital, after the army fled the provincial town.
"We expect to consolidate and have full control of the town later in the day," a senior rebel commander told Reuters in the southern mining capital of Lubumbashi.

But he said forces of the Presidential Guard, Mobutu's best equipped and trained troops, were strongly defending Kikwit airport which the rebels need as a springboard for the final assault on Kinshasa.
"There are problems around and towards the airport because the presidential guard is putting up stiff resistance," he said.
Thousands of jubilant Kikwit residents greeted the rebels, one witness said.

Richardson, seeking a negotiated end to Zaire's civil war, met Mobutu at his presidential villa inside Kinshasa's heavily defended Camp Tshatshi by the Zaire River. He was due to fly to Lubumbashi later on Tuesday for talks with Kabila.
"We're here to stress that the two sides need to talk," Richardson's spokesman Calvin Mitchell told reporters.
"The question of the venue is something that all the parties including South Africa, the United Nations and the OAU (Organisation of African Unity) have been working on."
Mobutu, who has cancer, has ruled out South Africa as too far on health grounds. Kabila has ruled out Congo's capital Brazzaville, over the river from Kinshasa, on security grounds.

Gabon has offered to host the talks. South Africa's Business Day newspaper reported on Tuesday that a South African naval supply ship, the Outeniqua, could host the talks off Zaire or Angola's neighbouring Cabinda enclave.

Mitchell said Richardson, who is also keen to ease the plight of dying Rwandan Hutu refugees in rebel-held areas, would spend Tuesday night in Lubumbashi and visit rebel-held Kisangani, north of the refugee zone, on Wednesday.

He said that Richardson also planned to visit Angola, which Zaire has accused of invading its territory in support of the rebels. "We plan to go there (Angola) but obviously the ambassador is flexible about timing," Mitchell said.
The provisional plan was to visit Angola on Thursday.

Diplomatic sources said there was concern that Angola, struggling to establish its own fragile peace process, could be sucked into the Zaire war with government forces backing the rebels and former UNITA rebels backing the Zairean government.
The rebels, who took up arms in October, now control over half of Zaire, a sprawling nation at the heart of Africa.
Mobutu, who had prostate cancer surgery in Europe in August, did not appear in public before Tuesday's talks. The veteran strongman has not been seen in public for over two weeks.
Richardson has called for a settlement "leading to an inclusive transitional government and fair and free elections".
He is also focusing on the plight of thousands of refugees and displaced Zaireans. "There is a humanitarian crisis here and the international community must respond," he said on Monday.
The rebels have been accused of driving the Rwandan Hutu refugees into the jungle in the hope that they die there. Kabila has given aid agencies 60 days to repatriate the Rwandans.
Thousands of Rwandan Hutus returned to Biaro camp south of Kisangani on Monday, telling of a horrific slaughter last week.
Dozens of corpses of those too sick to flee fighting between Hutu refugees, local Zaireans and rebel soldiers there last week lay festering in the camp, 45 km (25 miles) south of Kisangani.
